newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends up amid weather, line plan.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends up amid weather, line plan.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures settled sharply higher Friday amid forecasts of above-normal temperatures across the West and proposals to lower capacity on the Pacific Intertie in early July.
The revised forecasts, intertie talk as well as higher natural gas futures shook the complex out of its recent rangebound activity, market sources said.
July Palo Verde (PV) futures settled up 92 cents at $27.62 a megawatt hour (MWh) after hitting resistance at $28.00.
August PV finished up 95 cents at $29.86. Deferred PV months ended 10 to 25 cents higher.
July California-Oregon Border (COB) futures settled up 72 cents at $17.80 a megawatt hour (MWh) after posting a session high at $18.10.
August COB finished up 32 cents at $20.91. Other active COB ended up 10 to 35 cents higher.
Bonneville Power Administration said it proposes intertie transmission capacity for the summer to be reduced to 6,300 megawatts (MW) from the current limit of 7,200 MW.
Next week, a Western Systems Coordinating Council committee is expected to propose a summertime intertie rating of 6,900 MW, only 300 MW below from current level.
Some traders, baffled by the rise in COB, said a proposed intertie reduction would increase summer power supply rise in the Northwest, which is considered bearish for COB values.
Some meteorolgists revised their six to 10 day forecasts for West calling for above normal temperatures rather than seasonal readings.
NYMEX July Henry Hub natgas futures settled up 6.9 cents at $2.149 cents per million British thermal units.
Despite strength in futures prices, spot physical prices continued this week's weakness on moderate weather, ample hydropower supply and increasing coal-fired generation.
Firm, peak power prices for Monday at PV fell to $19.50-20.50 from yesterday's $21.00-22.50, while those at COB notched down to $14.00-15.00 from $14.50-15.50 Thursday.
Over 2,500 MW of generation was expected to return to service by next week.

Several Western coal-fired power units began restarting yesterday, including a 450 MW San Juan unit in New Mexico, a 300 MW Reid Gardner unit in Nevada, a 190 MW Hayden unit in Colorado and a 670 MW Centralia unit in Washington.
In addition, the 1,112 MW WNP-2 nuclear power plant in Washington state was expected to resume power production next week, ahead of an original schedule.
Meanwhile, a 875 MW unit at the Intermountain coal-fired power plant in Utah is said to shut today through Sunday to repair a tube leak.
The 750 MW unit 5 at the Four Corners coal-fired power plant in New Mexico was expected to return to service by Monday following a shutdown late Thursday.
Market sources said today's rise is vulnerable to a correction Monday.
"If daily prices don't come up...this thing could come right off," said a Houston futures trader.
NYMEX estimated 662 COB and 573 PV contracts were sold.
((--R Leong, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1622))
